entry.title: From Project Documents to Organizational Knowledge: Lessons from a Year in Project Control

link.title: From Project Documents to Organizational Knowledge: Lessons from a Year in Project Control

entry.content:
When I graduated with a Bachelor’s degree in Information Systems, I did not expect my first professional experience to teach me so much about information itself.

I began working as a Project Control Administrator (PPC) in mid-2025, about a month after completing my undergraduate studies. Since PPC roles in my work environment were largely associated with engineering and civil engineering backgrounds, I initially imagined that I would spend much of my time in the field, working with quantities and project measurements.

The reality was somewhat different.

My work involved a combination of project documentation, reporting, approval tracking, claim-related work, quantity information, archiving, Excel-based data handling, and coordination with project teams. At first, many of these activities felt unfamiliar. But over time, I gradually became part of the workflow and learned how these pieces of information connect throughout a project.

What initially seemed like administrative work eventually gave me a different perspective on how organizations manage information.

Learning Through Project Control

Project control is not only about monitoring whether work is progressing according to plan.

In practice, it also involves continuously working with information:

  • What work has been completed?
  • When was it completed?
  • How much has been completed?
  • Which work item or activity does it belong to?
  • What evidence supports the reported progress?
  • What is planned next?
  • Are there any concerns or issues that need to be followed up?

These questions appear simple, but answering them reliably depends on the availability and continuity of project records.

During my first year, I worked with different types of project information and gradually became more aware that the usefulness of information depends not only on whether it exists, but also on whether it can still be found, understood, and connected to the context in which it was created.

When Historical Information Became a Problem

One experience particularly changed the way I thought about project documentation.

At one point, I was asked to prepare historical weekly and monthly project reports for a project that was already approaching completion.

The challenge was that I had not been part of the project during its earlier stages. By the time I joined, much of the project was already underway, and some of the earlier reporting records were incomplete.

The reports needed to describe project progress over time, including information such as daily activities, quantities, completed work items, dates, progress, supporting evidence, photographs, upcoming plans, and concerns.

So I started by looking for whatever information was still available.

I went through the remaining project records and tried to connect the available pieces of information. I compared progress data, quantities, work items, dates, and other supporting records to understand what had most likely happened during the earlier stages of the project.

Some evidence was limited.

Some progress photographs were no longer available. Some of the earlier records were incomplete. The people who had previously handled parts of the project were no longer available to provide additional context, and even the earlier stages of the project had not necessarily been managed by the same person.

As a result, I had to reconstruct the reports using the evidence that remained.

It was not a perfect reconstruction. It could not be, because the original information was incomplete.

Instead, I tried to build the most reasonable representation possible from the available records by comparing different sources and checking whether the information was consistent with the progress that could still be observed from the remaining data.

That experience stayed with me.

Information Has Value Beyond the Moment It Is Created

Before working in industry, I mostly encountered information management through university courses, research, datasets, and academic projects.

Working in a real project environment made the issue feel much more tangible.

A progress record may seem routine when a project is running normally. A daily report may simply feel like another document that needs to be completed. A photograph may appear to be just another piece of project evidence.

But their value can change over time.

When a project approaches completion and someone needs to understand what happened months earlier, those seemingly routine records can become essential evidence.

This made me realize that the problem is not always that an organization has too little information.

Sometimes, the information may have existed but was not preserved in a way that makes it easy to retrieve, interpret, and use later.

Project closeout practices similarly emphasize the importance of preserving project records and historical information for future reference, analysis, and organizational learning.

What Information Systems Looks Like in Practice

This experience also changed the way I viewed my undergraduate background in Information Systems.

At university, I learned about data, information, systems, analysis, and research methods. It was easy to imagine that organizations would naturally have established ways to organize and manage their information.

Industry showed me a more complicated reality.

Organizations operate under different priorities. In a project environment, immediate operational demands may naturally receive more attention than information that appears to have little immediate value.

The importance of some information may only become obvious later.

This does not necessarily mean that an organization is poor at information management. Rather, it made me realize that information management is closely connected to organizational context, operational priorities, and the way work is actually carried out.

That was an important lesson for me as an Information Systems graduate.

From Reconstruction to Prevention

After going through this experience, I started thinking about a simple question:

Why should important project information be reconstructed only when it becomes urgently needed?

If certain information is likely to become important during project review or closeout, perhaps it should already be organized and preserved from the beginning.

Instead of waiting until the end of a project to determine which records are still useful, organizations could establish clearer practices for identifying, retaining, and organizing important information throughout the project lifecycle.

This does not necessarily mean keeping everything.

The more useful question may be:

What information should we preserve, why might it matter later, and how can we make it accessible when it is needed?

This way of thinking gradually moved my attention from simply managing documents toward thinking about information as organizational knowledge.

Connecting Practice with Research

My interest in Artificial Intelligence, Digital Knowledge Management (DKM), and Project Management Information Systems (PMIS) did not begin entirely from this work experience.

I had already encountered these topics through academic research, particularly through studies and examples from international research communities.

However, working in project control gave those concepts a much more concrete context.

I began to see that the challenges discussed in research are not always abstract technological problems. They can appear in ordinary organizational activities: finding historical information, connecting fragmented records, understanding what happened earlier in a project, and ensuring that useful information remains available when people need it.

This experience strengthened my interest in exploring how information systems and emerging technologies can help organizations manage knowledge more effectively.

Artificial Intelligence, for example, may eventually assist organizations in retrieving, organizing, summarizing, or transforming large amounts of project information into more usable forms.

But technology alone is not enough.

The underlying information still needs to be captured, structured, contextualized, and validated.

That is where I see the connection between technology, knowledge management, and organizational decision-making.

Looking Back After a Year

My first year in project control was not what I originally imagined when I graduated.

I expected to learn about project work.

Instead, I also learned about the lifecycle of information.

I learned that information can become valuable long after it is created. I learned that incomplete records can create significant work later. And I learned that the challenge is not always about having more data, but about making sure that the right information can still be found, understood, and trusted when it matters.

Most importantly, the experience gave practical meaning to something I had previously encountered mainly through academic study.

Information is not only something organizations collect. It is something they need to preserve, connect, and make useful over time.

This perspective continues to shape my interest in Artificial Intelligence, Digital Knowledge Management, and Project Management Information Systems as I explore how technology can support better information use and decision-making in knowledge-intensive organizations.

One year in project control, and a different way of seeing information.
entry.summary: Reflections on how a year in project control changed my understanding of project information, documentation, and organizational knowledge.

entry.title: AI-Assisted Systematic Literature Reviews: A Practical Exploration with Python

link.title: AI-Assisted Systematic Literature Reviews: A Practical Exploration with Python

entry.content:
Systematic Literature Reviews (SLRs) are widely used to provide rigorous evidence synthesis in academic research. By systematically identifying, screening, evaluating, and synthesizing prior studies, SLRs provide a rigorous foundation for theoretical development and empirical inquiry.

However, conducting an SLR is notoriously time-consuming, cognitively demanding, and methodologically complex.

Recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly in machine learning and natural language processing (NLP), are reshaping how researchers approach knowledge synthesis.

The Challenge of Traditional SLRs

A conventional SLR typically involves:

  1. Defining research questions
  2. Designing search strategies
  3. Screening titles and abstracts
  4. Conducting full-text eligibility assessment
  5. Extracting structured data
  6. Performing quality appraisal
  7. Synthesizing findings

When datasets involve hundreds or thousands of publications, manual screening can become a major bottleneck.

AI has the potential to significantly reduce review time while supporting methodological rigor — provided it is implemented responsibly.

How AI Transforms the SLR Workflow

Figure 1. AI-Assisted Systematic Literature Review Framework.

AI does not replace researchers. Instead, it augments specific stages of the review process.

1️⃣ Automated Screening

Supervised machine learning and NLP models can classify abstracts according to predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. Such approaches can reduce the manual burden of screening large numbers of records while supporting consistent application of screening criteria.

2️⃣ Structured Data Extraction

Text-mining pipelines can assist in extracting:

  • Research objectives
  • Methodological approaches
  • Sample characteristics
  • Key findings

This can improve coding consistency and reduce researcher fatigue during large-scale reviews.

3️⃣ Semantic Synthesis and Gap Detection

Large Language Models (LLMs) can support:

  • Thematic clustering
  • Trend detection
  • Cross-study comparison
  • Research gap identification

Such capabilities can accelerate the transition from data collection to analytical insight.

Human-in-the-Loop: Preserving Rigor

Despite these advantages, AI-assisted SLRs require a human-in-the-loop approach.

Algorithmic bias, hallucinated outputs, and limited model transparency remain important methodological concerns. Therefore, AI should function as a decision-support tool rather than an autonomous reviewer.

Maintaining transparency, validation checkpoints, and reproducibility protocols helps preserve academic rigor.

Practical Implementation with Python

Demonstration: Automated Screening in Practice

The dataset used in this demonstration originates from a bibliographic extraction conducted for my previously published study on Digital Knowledge Management in Project-Based Organizations.

For compliance reasons, the original dataset is not publicly shared. The example below illustrates the execution logic of an automated keyword-based screening function using a sample metadata file.

Python Execution

import pandas as pd

def ai_assisted_screening(dataset_path, keywords):
    df = pd.read_csv(dataset_path)
    mask = df['Abstract'].str.contains('|'.join(keywords), case=False, na=False)
    relevant_papers = df[mask]
    
    print(f"Total relevant papers found: {len(relevant_papers)}")
    return relevant_papers

# Example usage:
# keywords = ['Artificial Intelligence', 'Automation', 'NLP']
# relevant_df = ai_assisted_screening('sample_metadata.csv', keywords)

Dataset Reduction Impact

The automated keyword screening substantially reduced the dataset size, demonstrating how automated filtering can support efficient evidence triage in large bibliographic corpora.

In this demonstration, the dataset was reduced by approximately 88.44%, significantly narrowing the review scope to records matching the predefined keywords.

Such early-stage computational filtering enables researchers to allocate cognitive effort to higher-level analytical synthesis rather than mechanical exclusion tasks.

Stopword Filtering and Thematic Signal Extraction

After stopword removal and text normalization, thematic signal extraction reveals dominant research terms across the screened abstracts.

High-frequency non-informative words (e.g., the, and, of, to, in) were filtered to enhance interpretability and analytical clarity. The resulting keyword frequency distribution provides a clearer view of the dominant terms in the screened dataset.

This step strengthens transparency and reproducibility by helping ensure that visualized patterns reflect substantive research terms rather than common linguistic artifacts.

From Automation to Augmentation

This methodological experimentation builds upon prior empirical work and reflects an ongoing exploration of AI-assisted research workflows.

Rather than replacing scholarly judgment, AI serves as a computational amplifier — accelerating screening, enhancing thematic clarity, and supporting reproducible analytical pipelines.

When implemented responsibly within a human-in-the-loop framework, AI can help transform Systematic Literature Reviews from a predominantly manual endeavor into a more scalable, data-informed, and methodologically transparent research process.

References & Acknowledgement

The phrase “Cheap, Quick, and Rigorous” is drawn from methodological discussions of AI-assisted systematic reviews. See: Atkinson, C. F. (2023). Cheap, Quick, and Rigorous: Artificial Intelligence and the Systematic Literature Review. Social Science Computer Review, 42(2), 376–393. https://doi.org/10.1177/08944393231196281 This blog post reflects a practical and exploratory extension of that broader discussion.
entry.summary: Exploring how Artificial Intelligence and Python-based automation can support the rigor and efficiency of Systematic Literature Reviews.

entry.title: Finding My Place
entry.content:
When I first entered university, I remember feeling small.
The classroom was full of new faces, and I didn’t know anyone in my class.
For a moment, I wondered whether I would be able to make friends or feel like I belonged here.

But slowly, things opened up.
I made friends who were warm, patient, and genuine.
I learned how to speak up more, how to start conversations, and how to step forward even when I felt unsure.

Originally, I wanted to study Design, because I loved drawing.
But my parents encouraged me to choose a major that felt more “clear” and practical, so I entered Information Systems.

At first, it felt like a compromise.
But over time, I understood that I actually enjoy technology.
Not the heavy coding part (I still laugh at myself there),
but the idea of helping people work better through systems and information.

It turns out, this path fits me too.

My interest in technology and AI grew around my fifth semester, especially when I began thinking about internships and my thesis.

Around the same time, I was also improving my English.
I started as a learner, then became a co-mentor, and eventually a mentor.
It was funny, because I still felt my English was far from perfect.

But teaching taught me how to stay humble, keep learning, and stay connected.
I met students and fellow mentors from many places.
Some of them, I still keep in touch with today.

There were many small moments that made my university life feel alive.
Laughing with friends, late group projects, and warm conversations with lecturers who felt more like companions than strict authority figures.

And yes — I once got totally lost in Singapore.

I panicked for a while, but looking back, it’s one of the funniest memories I have.
Traveling, learning, getting lost, finding my way — it all became part of who I am.

If I could summarize my journey in one word, it would be:

Growing.

Not fast.
Not loud.
But steady, warm, and real.
entry.summary: A little memory from when I first entered university.

entry.title: Academic Visit to NUS: Observations from the Information Systems and Analytics Research Labs

link.title: Academic Visit to NUS: Observations from the Information Systems and Analytics Research Labs

entry.content:
“Observing the intersection of rigorous methodology and practical innovation at the National University of Singapore.”

Academic Visit to the Information Systems and Analytics Research Labs

Department of Information Systems and Analytics, NUS.

In late 2023, I conducted an academic visit to the National University of Singapore (NUS), specifically targeting the Department of Information Systems and Analytics (DISA). The primary objective was to observe and learn from the research environment and infrastructure within the Information Systems and Analytics Research Labs. During the session, I was guided by a PhD researcher who provided an overview of the lab’s research activities and environment. The discussion focused on several key areas:

  • Research Integration: How Information Systems research connects theoretical perspectives with practical problems.
  • Collaborative Ecosystem: How doctoral researchers and faculty members interact within a research-oriented environment.
  • Data-Driven Innovation: How analytics and information systems research can contribute to organizational and technological development.


Developing Academic Resilience

Visiting a leading academic institution in Asia gave me a valuable perspective on academic resilience. The visit also reminded me of the importance of adaptability and the ability to engage in academic discussions across diverse backgrounds. This experience reinforced the importance of proactive inquiry and persistence—qualities that are essential for any researcher striving to contribute to the international scientific community.

Alignment with Research Objectives

The visit to the Information Systems and Analytics Research Labs provided important perspectives on how technology can align with organizational goals. This experience directed my research interests toward exploring Digital Transformation in Organizations and Digital Knowledge Management (DKM).

Although I began my research exploration by studying technical capabilities such as AI and NLP, my focus has now shifted toward a more strategic direction. I want to understand how these technologies are actually implemented to support organizational success. Through the Systematic Literature Review (SLR) method, I seek to bridge the potential of technology with practical management needs—an approach that aligns with my background in Information Systems.

Conclusion

This visit became an important reference point in my academic and professional development. It continues to shape how I think about bridging academic theory with practical challenges in industry.

“A commitment to excellence, inspired by global research standards.”

Personal reflection on an academic visit to the National University of Singapore.
entry.summary: An observational study of the research ecosystem within the Department of Information Systems and Analytics (DISA), NUS.

entry.title: My First Days in Singapore 🇸🇬
entry.content:
“Sometimes, a place gently teaches you who you could become.”

Arrival — Day 1

The first steps outside the airport felt different.
The air was clean. The atmosphere was organized.
People walked with calm confidence.
I paused — not because I was confused, but because I was quietly absorbing everything.

That day, I checked in at Spacepod @Lavender, a small capsule hotel.
It was simple, warm, and exactly what I needed after traveling.

I rested.
I let myself breathe.
And in that silence, I whispered softly:

“Grow — slowly, softly, but continuously.”


Day 1 Evening — Quiet Space to Reset

The capsule felt like my own little cocoon.
A place to reset.
A place to be still with my thoughts.

Even though I didn’t do much on the first day,
my mind was already learning something new:

Peace is also progress.


Day 2 — A Little Adventure Begins

We woke up early to visit NTU and NUS.
But of course — adventure comes with stories 😄 Our group got lost trying to find NTU.
Nearly two hours of rerouting, guessing, asking strangers, trying again.

The funny part is: most of us weren’t confident speaking English,
but we held onto one motto:

“Malu bertanya sesat di jalan.”

So we asked.
Smiled awkwardly.
Got confused again.
Laughed.
And kept going.

And eventually — we made it.
Tired, a little embarrassed, but proud.

Sometimes the journey teaches more than the destination.

Merlion & Gardens by the Bay

Later that evening, we visited Merlion and Gardens by the Bay.
I didn’t take many photos.
I just let myself exist there — present and quiet.

City lights reflecting on the water.
The warm breeze.
People laughing.
Life moving gently.

In that moment, I felt small —
but in a way that opened space inside me.


Reflection 🌿

Singapore didn’t change me overnight.
But it showed me something:

There is a version of me
who is more confident, calmer, and more open to the world —
and she is possible.

Note to My Future Self

If one day you return here,
come as someone who has grown enough to say:

“Thank you for inspiring me to try harder — softly, but consistently.”

written with warm memory
entry.summary: A quiet memory of arriving, learning, and getting a little braver.
